description: A horizontally scalable, Jellyfin-compatible video server in Go. Every task below comes from PRODUCT.md (features and roadmap), the project plan, compat/coverage-12.4.tsv and the agreed work queue. PRODUCT.md stays the source of truth for status; update this file when a slice merges.

conventions.status: done | in_progress | todo; passes is true only when done
conventions.priority: 1 is next; done tasks have none
conventions.delivery: each task goes through the build workflow (.claude/workflows/build.js): checks written first and locked, one implementer until they pass, QA and one blind adversarial review with evidence-gated findings, one fix round; then PR, CI, merge, redeploy the dogfood
conventions.differential: a task that adds or changes a route jellyfin-web or another client calls adds its requests to test/differential/requests.yaml, and any difference it keeps to compat/differences.yaml with a reason

userStories.title: Follow any playback end to end, and see why the cluster needed more workers
userStories.description: An operator must be able to see exactly where a playback stalled and why the cluster needed more workers, not only that a film is transcoding. Metrics (JS-019) give totals: stalls happened, the queue is deep. This adds one OpenTelemetry trace per playback (PlaySessionId) across the api, stream and worker processes: PlaybackInfo and its decision with reasons; each segment request and where its time went (served from the store, waited on a job, started a job); the job queued, claimed (queue time, which worker) and its ffmpeg runs with their speed; helpers started, and helpers wanted but not started for lack of a free slot; and a failover (lock lost, reap, replacement). The reasons for more workers become metrics too, which autoscaling (JS-057) scales on, so the reason it scaled is visible. Viewers keep seeing in their app that a film is transcoding and why (JS-067).
acceptanceCriteria: One trace per playback session spans the api, stream and worker processes, its context carried in the transcode job row across the Postgres handoff

Given a stalled segment (over 5 s), its trace shows which part took the time: waiting for a free slot, an encode slower than real time, the upload, or reading the store; the stall metric links to the trace (exemplar)
A failover shows the dead worker's span end and the replacement's begin in one trace
Helper decisions are traced and counted: helpers started with the job's speed, and helpers wanted but not started because no slot was free

Demand for workers is a metric with its reason (jobs waiting for a slot and how long, helpers wanted but refused, jobs below real time), and the autoscaler's input is one of these, so why the cluster grew can be read back
Log lines carry the trace id (JS-022), so a trace leads to its logs
jellyfin-web's playback info still shows transcoding, its reasons and speed (JS-067), and stays right while helpers run (the viewer's own job may have ended)
Exported over OTLP to any backend, off by default; the dogfood runs a backend and the docs show reading a stall from it
Checked with real processes: a test collector receives a playback's trace from three processes, with a stall and a failover in it
userStories.notes: Needs a design review; the homelab has no tracing backend yet (Tempo suggested). Product owner (2026-11-08): wants to trace everything through the pipeline, see where something stalled and why more workers were needed; placed before P6 (Kubernetes). JS-024 review (UX): Sessions can show the viewer's job as done while helpers encode, and no log line says a helper started.

userStories.title: Dolby Vision and HDR labels and the decisions that follow from them
userStories.description: Report VideoRange and VideoRangeType as Jellyfin 12.4 does (DOVI for P5, DOVIWithEL for P7, DOVIWithHDR10, DOVIWithHLG and DOVIWithSDR for P8 by base-layer compatibility, HDR10Plus and the DOVI-with-HDR10+ variants), stop stripping them from client DTOs, and use them in the playback decision: a client whose profile allows HDR10 (or HLG, or SDR) but not Dolby Vision plays a DV file whose base layer it supports, instead of a re-encode.
acceptanceCriteria: Observed against a real Jellyfin 12.4 first (synthetic DV fixtures in a disposable jellyfin/jellyfin:12.4 container): item DTOs, PlaybackInfo decisions and the master playlist's codec tag for P5, P7 and P8.1; capture in compat/captures
The scan records the DV profile, base-layer compatibility id and HDR10+ presence
Item and PlaybackInfo DTOs carry VideoRange and VideoRangeType for SDR, HDR10, HDR10Plus, HLG and each DV variant

A profile that allows HDR10 but no DOVI type direct plays or copies a P8.1 file as HDR10; one that allows nothing HDR re-encodes with tone mapping as today; P5 (no compatible base layer) is never sent to a client without DV
The decision table tests cover every VideoRangeType against jellyfin-web's own profile conditions
Checked on the dogfood with a P8.1 film and a P7 film in jellyfin-web and one TV client
userStories.source: work queue 4; internal/library/scan.go strips them today
userStories.notes: Found while preparing the task (2026-11-07): Jellyfin's labels drive decisions, not only display. jellyfin-web sends CodecProfiles conditions on VideoRangeType, and Jellyfin copies a DOVIWithHDR10 stream to an HDR10-only client (tagging it db1p in the master playlist). jellyscale reports every DV file as plain DOVI, so those films are re-encoded in software today. Built 2026-11-08: Jellyfin 12.4 labels P8 compat 0 as DOVIInvalid and compat 3 as plain HDR10, and copies a DV file whose base layer the client plays as a transcode with VideoRangeTypeNotSupported (video copied, base layer in CODECS/VIDEO-RANGE, DV brand in SUPPLEMENTAL-CODECS) rather than direct play. The fixtures carry only the dvcC box (no RPUs). The lead checks real P8.1 and P7 films in jellyfin-web on the dogfood after merge; TV clients wait for the client pivot (JS-070, JS-065). Backlog: a row scanned before this change is not tone mapped until the next scan re-probes it; a failed HDR10+ frame read leaves HDR10 until the file changes; no test copies a DV file through jellyscale's own ffmpeg path (Jellyfin's argument set drops dvcC from the init segment, checked by hand); an old api replica refuses the HEVC copy a new one offers during a rollout.

userStories.title: Parallel transcoding of one stream across workers
userStories.description: When a job runs below about 1.2x real time, helper jobs on other workers encode later chunks of the same film, so CPU on every node serves one viewer. Deterministic segments let the chunks splice.
acceptanceCriteria: Design reviewed before building (chunk boundaries, slots, cancellation, read-ahead, failover of a helper)
Three worker processes encode one film in chunks; the assembled segments equal a single worker's video byte for byte
hls.js plays through and seeks across chunk boundaries with no stall or discontinuity
A helper killed mid-chunk is replaced and the viewer keeps playing
Helpers never take the last free slot from a new viewer
Measured speedup with 1, 2 and 3 workers in the PR
userStories.notes: The user's idea: use CPU on all nodes rather than relying on a GPU. 'Gotta test sharding streams.' Built 2026-11-08: a job below 1.2x real time (judged after 2 s of output) inserts a helper row for the next free 4-segment chunk within the viewer's lead; helpers are claimed by other workers first and never take a worker's last free slot. A job's ffmpeg runs on across chunk starts until it reaches a chunk another job holds, so a job nobody helps is one ffmpeg. Measured with each worker's ffmpeg pinned to one CPU: 1 worker 16.3 s, 2 workers 10.4 s (1.57x), 3 workers 8.0 s (2.03x). Re-encoded segments from different runs have the same frames and frame times within 1 ms, not the same bytes (x264 stays multi-threaded). A burnt image subtitle gets no helpers (a run that starts mid-film loses the cue showing at its start); JS-071 closes that gap. A failed helper does not fail the viewer's spec and blocks re-helping its chunk for 30 s. Backlog: helpers are a fixed threshold (1.2x), not a measure of spare capacity across the cluster; a helper's chunk that the viewer never reaches is wasted work until the idle kill; per-helper metrics (JS-021 traces should show which chunks were helped and why).

userStories.title: Copy HDR video and re-encode only the audio
userStories.description: A client that plays the HDR video but not its audio (TrueHD, DTS in jellyfin-web) gets the video copied and the audio re-encoded, instead of a full 4K software re-encode with tone mapping.
acceptanceCriteria: HDR10, HLG and DV (with a compatible base layer) copy when the client's profile allows
jellyfin-web plays a 4K HDR film with TrueHD audio from a copy on a 4-core worker without stalls
Tone mapping stays for clients that cannot show HDR

An integration test copies HDR10, HLG, DV 8.1 and DV 7 fixtures through the worker's own ffmpeg path and checks each init segment's sample entry (hvc1, no dvcC/dvvC where the DV layer is dropped) and the master's VIDEO-RANGE
A rolling update cannot break playback: a stream replica serves every copy an api replica of the same or the previous release offers, or docs/running.md states the roll order and a test pins it
userStories.source: work queue 6; PRODUCT.md phase3 (HDR direct play and copy not built)
userStories.notes: Added after JS-023 (2026-11-08): JS-023 decides DV copies and writes the master, but no test runs a copy through jellyscale's ffmpeg (Jellyfin's arguments drop dvcC, checked by hand only), and its review found that an old replica refuses the HEVC copy a new one offers mid-rollout. Plain HDR copy widens both risks, so they belong here. Built 2026-11-08: CanCopy and canServeCopy accept HDR10, HDR10+ and HLG in HEVC and AV1 (not H.264, not an unscanned range); the master names PQ or HLG, and cdm4 for HDR10+, matching a Jellyfin 12.4 capture (compat/captures/hdr-copy-12.4.md) for 3 films under 6 profiles. A profile that cannot show the range is still tone mapped. An integration test copies HDR10, HLG, DV 8.1 and DV 7 through the worker's own ffmpeg and checks the init segment (hvc1, no dvcC/dvvC, transfer kept). Roll order: stream replicas first (docs/running.md). Measured by the lead: a 4K HDR10 HEVC film with 5.1 TrueHD copies at about 73x real time on 4 CPUs (30 s in 0.41 s). Backlog: no automated check of a 4K TrueHD copy; the e2e copy scenario needs E2E_HEVC=1 so it never runs in CI (CI's Chrome plays AV1, so an AV1 HDR10 copy scenario could); no ffmpeg-path test of an AV1 HDR copy; the DV 7 fixture has no enhancement-layer NALs; the roll-order check pins wording; the capture note's TrueHD observation is not in its JSON.

userStories.title: Copy both video and audio
userStories.description: Remux into HLS without re-encoding either stream when the client plays both but not the container.
acceptanceCriteria: Video and audio both copied, segments splice after a restart
Played and sought in jellyfin-web
userStories.notes: Built 2026-11-09. Observed on a real Jellyfin 12.4 first (compat/captures/copy-both-12.4.md): Remux copies both when the fMP4 HLS profile takes the audio codec and channels. jellyscale copies the track under the audio-copy rules (codec in the URL's list, channels within the limit, at most a quarter of the cap), else re-encodes it with the video still copied; a restart seeks the audio to the video's cut so segments splice on any worker (13 films, MKV and MP4, H.264, HEVC, AV1; AAC, AC3, E-AC3, MP3, Opus, FLAC). TranscodeReasons now add the codec reasons Jellyfin adds when the container is the reason. Played in jellyfin-web in Chrome by picking the AAC track of an H.264 and AC3 film. Two disputes upheld: a unit test pinning the replaced behaviour, and an e2e precondition that assumed a fresh job when segment reuse is correct. Backlog: SecondaryAudioNotSupported for a track pick, MP3 under Chrome (fMP4 only), the audio list for HEVC and AV1 copies comes from the H.264 HLS profile. Follow-up: JS-074 (read the film once).

userStories.description: One worker read of the file extracts every text track, instead of one job per track.
acceptanceCriteria: One ffmpeg run per film for all text tracks
S3 reads drop accordingly
userStories.notes: One subtitle_jobs row and one ffmpeg run per film write every text track inside it; a later pick of another track is served from the store. ffmpeg names the streams it fails on, so any number of undecodable tracks costs two reads, each with the whole limit; streams the file lacks are dropped at setup. A mark names the file version it was read from. Known limit: a track ffmpeg hangs on until the limit keeps the other tracks unstored. Three attempts.

userStories.title: Keep playback and transcodes through a Postgres failover
userStories.description: A CNPG switchover ends every worker's lock connection; today every transcode restarts. Re-lock first, then check the worker's own row: if it is present nobody touched its jobs and they continue. The stream role has the same failure: every playlist, segment and direct-play request reads Postgres (token, source row, viewer), and a database error is answered with a 500 (internal/api/server.go requireAuth, transcode.go, stream.go), which jellyfin-web treats as the end of playback (DOMAINS.md: any answer of 400 or more destroys the player). So a switchover, the most ordinary Kubernetes event, stops every viewer. The stream role must never answer 5xx for a database that is briefly away.
acceptanceCriteria: A Postgres restart or switchover under load does not restart transcodes whose rows survived
No job is ever owned by two workers (invariant 25)

A Postgres restart mid-film, for HLS and for direct play, in jellyfin-web in the e2e tier: the picture continues and no request is answered 5xx for the database's absence (the stream role waits within hls.js's retry window, or serves from a short in-process cache of tokens and source rows)
/healthz of the stream and api roles does not fail every replica at once when Postgres is away

userStories.title: Use every GPU and CPU the cluster has
userStories.description: A worker uses whatever encoder hardware its node exposes (NVIDIA NVENC, Intel QSV or VAAPI, AMD VAAPI) and falls back to the CPU, so a cluster with GPUs uses them, as Jellyfin does on the dogfood's Intel iGPUs. fMP4 can't splice across encoder families (spikes/seam: x264 spliced with NVENC lost half the frames), so each stream is given the best family with room when it starts, and its helpers (JS-024) and failover stay in that family. A GPU can also serve a CPU-encoded stream by decoding for it, if its frames equal software decoding, so every node still helps every stream.
acceptanceCriteria: Design reviewed before building: how a family is chosen for a stream, helpers and failover within a family, and what a viewer sees when the last worker of their stream's family is lost mid-film (playing on is the goal; a restart needs the product owner's decision); and whether a copy and a re-encode should share one slot pool (today a near-free copy holds a slot for the whole film like a multi-core re-encode)
A worker detects at start which encoders its node can run (a short test encode per family, not the ffmpeg build's list) and advertises them; a node with no GPU runs exactly as before
A new stream gets a GPU family when a worker of that family has a free slot, and the CPU otherwise; the encoder family stays in the spec hash and the decision is logged and metered with its reason
Helpers and failover of a GPU stream stay in its family; a seek, a restart and a helper's chunk splice cleanly on QSV/VAAPI and NVENC as the seam spike showed for one family
Hardware decoding for CPU-encoded streams only where its frames are measured equal to software decoding (per codec and family); otherwise software decoding

Tested on real hardware in its own tier chosen explicitly (never skipped): Intel QSV/VAAPI on the dogfood cluster's iGPUs and NVENC on a developer machine; jellyfin-web plays, seeks and recovers from a killed GPU worker
Operators see which encoder family and worker serve each stream (Sessions, metrics, JS-021 traces)
userStories.source: PRODUCT.md phase5-library; rewritten 2026-11-08: the product owner wants every GPU and CPU in the cluster used where possible, priority kept in P5
userStories.notes: The dogfood cluster has an Intel iGPU on each of its three nodes (gpu.intel.com/i915: 1 allocatable) and the user's Jellyfin requests one; the developer machine has an RTX 4070 Ti and an AMD iGPU. GPU tone mapping (libplacebo or vendor filters) gives frames unlike zscale's, so it splices only within its own family.

userStories.title: Burnt image subtitles in every run: helpers, seeks and failovers draw the cue that is showing
userStories.description: A PGS, VobSub or DVB cue is one packet when it appears, so an ffmpeg that begins mid-film (a seek, a failover, a helper's chunk) never sees the cue already on screen and leaves it out until the next one (DOMAINS 51's known departure). JS-024 therefore gives burnt image subtitles no helpers: a slow 4K film with Blu-ray subtitles stalls on one worker as before. PRODUCT.md (The experience we're building) promises that every film gets every capability. Make a run that begins at segment N draw the cue showing at N: start its ffmpeg early enough to read that cue's packet (the packet time comes from the track itself, read once and cached like the PGS file copy) and drop the frames before N, or another way that keeps the segment's frames at a single run's times. Then let burnt image subtitles be chunked and helped like any slow re-encode.
acceptanceCriteria: Every run that begins at a segment N > 0 inside a burnt image cue draws, from its first frame until the cue ends, the picture a run from zero draws there, for each of PGS, VobSub and DVB; shown for a seek, a failover restart and a helper's chunk, each through a worker's job (TestBurnedImageSubtitleIsAtTheRightTime without its known-departure case)

The same holds for a cue that began long before the cut (50 s or more, several chunks back), on a film the scan has read, with the cue times reaching the run as they do in production and never handed in by the test
The same holds for a film whose index the scan does not read today: MPEG-2 video with a VobSub track in Matroska (a DVD rip)

With several cues in the film a run draws only what a run from zero shows at its cut: nothing in the gap after a cue has ended, before the first cue or after the last, and the later cue (not the earlier) when it begins inside the second of two
A PGS picture built by more than one packet (a line added while an earlier line stays on screen) is drawn whole by a run that begins after the later packet, as a run from zero draws it

A run that begins where no cue is showing, 50 s or more after the last cue ended, reads no more bytes of the film before its first segment than the same run without the track (within the spread of repeated runs), for each of PGS (ended by a clear packet), VobSub (ended by its duration) and DVB (whose clear packet carries a duration); measured through a worker's job

A run that begins inside a cue reads, beyond the same run without the track, at most the film from that cue's first packet to the cut; checked for a cue 8 s old and one 50 s old through a worker's job with the cue times as production supplies them, and the bound does not grow with the gap before the cue
A run from segment 0, and a run whose image track is a file beside the film, read nothing they do not read today

No job (from zero, a seek, a failover or a helper) starts or waits on a read of the whole film, or any read that grows with the film's length, to learn cue times: the first mid-film run on a film reads the same before its first segment for the same cue in a film four times as long
Two runs of one film that begin at once on two workers (two helpers, or a helper and a seek) each stay within one run's bound, and neither waits for a read the other makes

If learning the cue times takes a read that fails for a reason that is not the film's (a store error, a timeout, the job ending), the run does not go on as if nothing were showing: no segment is stored without a cue a run from zero draws, the failure is not remembered as the film's, and the read ends with its job

A film that lists no times for the track without a whole-film read (MPEG-TS; a Matroska written without cue points for the track) still starts no whole-film read: a mid-film run reads at most a stated look-back more than the run without the track, shows a cue that began within that look-back from its first frame, and an older cue is the one remaining gap, pinned by a test on both sides of the look-back
A film already in the library when the release is deployed (scanned by the previous release, its file unchanged) meets these criteria by the next scan at the latest, with no step by the operator
After a film's file is replaced by one whose cues fall at other times, a mid-film run draws and reads by the new file's cues, never the old file's

docs/transcoding.md records a seek's bytes read and time to first segment, measured through a worker on a film of stated size and bitrate, for origin/main and for this build: with no cue showing, inside a cue 8 s old and one 50 s old, and for the first mid-film run on a film as well as a later one; no check passes or fails on a duration

A slow re-encode with a burnt image subtitle, inside the film or in a file beside it, gets helpers as the same film without the track does (TestABurntImageSubtitleGetsNoHelpers inverted), with at least one helper's chunk beginning inside a cue and one beginning where nothing is showing

Every segment of that helped run has the same number of video frames at the same times (within 1 ms) as a single worker's run from zero, whichever run made it, and so does every segment a seek or a failover run makes

jellyfin-web plays a slow film with a burnt PGS track across a helper's chunk start that falls inside a cue: the cue is on screen before the chunk start, at the first frame played from the helper's segment and until the cue ends, that segment was made by the helper, and the player reports no error

DOMAINS 51's known departure, DOMAINS 58's exception for image subtitles and DOMAINS 22's exception for a PGS cue before a restart are removed, with ARCHITECTURE's Known departures and docs/status.md agreeing, and their replacement states the cost: where cue times come from and what that read costs per film and per run, a run's extra rea

85 (loadSeen), so a design that stores cue times at scan time covers only newly scanned films unless it adds a condition; DOMAINS 51's 'Upgrade' paragraph is the precedent. A design that reads near the cut at run time meets it trivially.
userStories.source: User decision 2026-11-08 during JS-024: no helpers for burnt image subtitles for now, and every film should eventually get every capability
userStories.notes: Built in two attempts. The scan keeps each image track's cue points from the Matroska Cues it already reads (media_sources.image_cues); a mid-film run reads the packet at the last point before its cut, opens at the start of the picture showing there and trims to the cut. Films with no points for the track (MPEG-TS, Matroska without Cues for it) open 10 s back. Burnt image subtitles now get helpers. A seek inside a cue costs about 0.3 MB and 0.04 s per second the cue has been showing (docs/transcoding.md); no cap (BL-049).

userStories.title: A new viewer never waits behind a helper
userStories.description: Helper jobs (JS-024) may fill every free transcode slot but one across the cluster and hold it until their chunk is done, so a second viewer who starts at the same moment queues behind them. A viewer's job takes a helper's slot instead: the helper stops, and its chunk falls back to the job that asked for help (or to another helper later). Operators can turn helpers off.
acceptanceCriteria: With every slot but one held by helpers, two new viewers start at the same moment on separate worker processes and both get their first segment as fast as with no helpers running
The preempted helper's chunk is still made: the helped viewer plays through it with no stall beyond what a seek costs
A helper is never preempted by another helper
An operator setting turns helpers off; with it off, a slow job is one ffmpeg and inserts no helper rows; documented in docs/running.md
No preemption ever stops a viewer's own job
userStories.source: JS-024 post-task review (2026-11-08); the user chose to land JS-024 and fix this next
userStories.notes: Found reading the helper slot guard after the build: freeSlots is cluster-wide, so helpers keep one slot free for the whole cluster, not per worker. Priority 2 puts it ahead of JS-025. Built 2026-11-08: a viewer's job, under the cluster-wide helpers lock, cancels one helper when no slot is free (a queued one first, else the one furthest ahead, only on a live worker), then sends a preempt hint after its transaction commits; a running helper beats on that hint, and once as it subscribes, so it gives its slot back at once rather than at its next heartbeat. Measured: with a paused helper, a 10 s heartbeat and the viewer arriving just after the helper beat, the viewer's first segment took 5.75 s, the same as on an idle cluster; without the hint it was refused. transcodeHelpers: false on a worker turns its helpers off. Backlog: every viewer's ensure takes the cluster-wide helpers lock; transcodeHelpers is per worker, so mixed settings are possible; no check drives the config key through to the worker; a helper preempted during its pre-ffmpeg setup (subtitle extraction, fonts) sees the cancel only after ffmpeg starts; when queued viewers already exceed the free slots, a new viewer still cancels a helper whose slot goes to an earlier viewer; the preempt hint names no job, so every running helper beats once per preemption; operators see preemption only in the job's error and the log.

userStories.title: A copy of both streams reads the film once
userStories.description: JS-026's copy of both opens the source twice, as a video copy with re-encoded audio does: the second input exists only so a re-encoded AAC track can start early on its own grid. A copied track needs neither, so the second open only doubles what a worker reads: ten times the film's bitrate while the job runs and twice its bytes per full watch, which on S3 is twice the egress and on a NAS twice the load. JS-026's design reviewer measured that one input splices the same segments.
acceptanceCriteria: A job copying both the video and the audio opens the source once: ffmpeg has one input, and on S3 the worker's range proxy serves one stream of the film's bytes, measured in a test with real ffmpeg

userStories.notes: JS-026's design reviewer ran a scratch experiment: one input at the copy's flags gave identical fragments to two inputs for H.264 with AC3 and E-AC3 in Matroska (13 of 13) and for AAC in MP4 after the first fragment. The implementer did not take it because JS-026's locked e2e helper reads the audio map from the second input (-map 1:N); this task changes that helper. Priority 5, right after JS-026: copies are the common path for a remux library, and halving their reads helps the S3 and NAS costs every copy-both viewer incurs. Built 2026-11-09: CopyCommand maps a copied audio track from the one input (-map 0:N); a copy with re-encoded audio keeps its two inputs. TestACopyOfBothStreamsFromS3ReadsTheFilmOnce measures the bytes the range proxy serves on SeaweedFS and Garage: 2.00 times the film before, once after (QA put the old command back and saw it fail). Every splice case of JS-026 still passes, AAC in MP4 byte for byte, under ffmpeg 9.0.2 and 6.1.1; the transcode e2e gate passed 60 of 60. userStories.title: Watch state survives a file missing from one scan, and libraries keep their identity
userStories.description: A scan deletes the item of every file the listing no longer shows, and a user's watch state cascades from the item (internal/library/scan.go, migration 0001 user_item_data ON DELETE CASCADE); a file that returns gets a new id. The only guard is a store that lists no video at all. So one disk of a pooled mount dropping out, a half-finished sync, a file replaced in two steps or an S3 re-upload under a new key loses positions, played flags and favourites for good, and changes ids clients hold. A library's id is a hash of its name, so renaming it in config creates a second library, and a library removed from config is never removed.
acceptanceCriteria: A file absent from a scan is hidden, not deleted, for a configurable grace (default days, not minutes), and a file that returns within it keeps its item id and every user's watch state
A file that reappears under another key with the same size and content identity (ETag, or the probe's fingerprint) inside the grace is matched to its old item across scans, not only within one
A scan that loses more than a set share of a library's files keeps them all and says so, as the empty-mount guard does
Renaming a library in config keeps its id and items; a library removed from config is hidden and later removed, documented in docs/running.md
Tests show each case loses no user_item_data row
userStories.notes: Must land before JS-045 starts P5 scan work and before JS-060 imports history.

userStories.title: Stream segments to the viewer without holding them whole in memory
userStories.description: The stream role reads every segment whole into memory before sending it (internal/transcode/jobs.go readSegment, io.ReadAll). A copied segment carries the file's bitrate and lasts up to 12 seconds (DOMAINS 47), so a 4K copy segment is tens of MB per request, times every concurrent viewer, and a stream pod's memory limit must be set to survive that. Send stored segments as they are read, keeping the guarantee that a cut or empty object is treated as not there yet.
acceptanceCriteria: A stored segment is sent while it is read; a segment cut short or empty is still re-asked rather than sent truncated
A test measures the stream role's peak memory for many concurrent viewers of a high-bitrate copy and states the bound
docs/running.md gives the stream role's memory per concurrent viewer, for JS-056's requests and limits

userStories.title: A size budget for the transcode store and cleanup of the asset store
userStories.description: The transcode store's segments are swept by age only, with no size budget and no metric of its size (internal/transcode/worker.go Sweep), and copies are stored at the file's own bitrate. The asset store is never cleaned: subtitle text, .sup copies and images of a changed or removed file stay for good (internal/subtitles/cache.go, sup.go, library/scan.go put with no delete).
acceptanceCriteria: The transcode store has a configurable size budget; past it the least recently used specs no viewer is watching are removed first; its size is a metric
Assets of a file version that no longer exists are removed by a sweep, with a test for subtitles, .sup copies and images
docs/running.md says how to size the transcode volume or bucket and what the sweep removes

userStories.title: Mixed versions are safe: migrations and spec hashes across a rolling upgrade
userStories.description: Every dogfood deploy already runs two versions side by side, but upgrade safety is one line at the end of the plan (JS-058). Migrations run with no lock timeout and no check for migrations a newer version applied (internal/db/db.go), an old worker can compute another spec hash than a new one (ARCHITECTURE.md known departures), and docs/running.md and ARCHITECTURE.md disagree on which role rolls first.
acceptanceCriteria: Migrations take a lock timeout and a version that finds a migration newer than it knows refuses to start with a clear message
A worker of the previous version and one of this version serve the same stream, in a real-process test, without a spec hash disagreement breaking playback (or the job is refused by the older one)
One documented rollout order, the same in docs/running.md and ARCHITECTURE.md, and a test or check that each migration in a release is safe for the previous version's code
userStories.notes: Before JS-054, which adds encoder families to the spec.

userStories.title: File naming against real library layouts: extras, specials and odd names
userStories.description: The naming rules have three tests (internal/library/naming_test.go) and every video in a movies library becomes a Movie (internal/library/scan.go), so extras, featurettes, trailers and samples beside a film are listed as films, and episodes without a season tag are skipped. Metadata files (JS-045) and the Jellyfin import (JS-060) attach to items by path, so the rules must be right first.
acceptanceCriteria: A table of real-world layouts (folders of extras, trailers, samples, specials, multi-episode files, years in names), from Jellyfin's documented naming conventions and observed on a real Jellyfin 12.4, with what each becomes
Extras are not listed as films; specials and season-less episodes are placed as Jellyfin 12.4 places them, or the difference is recorded
No library titles in the fixtures

userStories.title: Replace wall-clock ratio bars in tests with checks of the mechanism
userStories.description: Tests that pass or fail on a timing ratio are the largest class of merge-queue escapes (.results escape records for JS-067, JS-024 and JS-072): they pass on a 16-core developer machine and fail on shared CI runners. Convert the existing ratio bars (internal/transcode/helpers_integration_test.go and others found by grep) to checks of what the code does, such as how many helpers ran or which segments each made.
acceptanceCriteria: A timing bar is any assertion a slower runner can fail on a right build: a measured duration with an upper bound, two measured durations compared, or a measured speed with a lower bound or a not-slow flag. None is left in the Go tiers, test/e2e or test/roles.sh, and every assertion the grep finds that compares a measured time or speed is accounted for as replaced or as a hang bound, with the reason.

At least these are bars and are replaced. internal/transcode: helpers_integration_test.go (63 s for three workers; the 60/80/90% bars of TestMoreWorkersFinishTheFilmSooner; the 9 s slowest wait after a killed helper; the 9 s seek into a helper's chunk), helpers_preempt_integration_test.go (9 s slowest wait), hdrcopy_media_integration_test.go (10x real time), failover_integration_test.go (7 s from SIGKILL to the replacement's first segment), chapter_jobs_integration_test.go (2 s subtitle), metrics_integration_test.go (speed 0.6 to 1.5, twice). internal/api: transcoding_info_integration_test.go (EncodeSpeed 0.1 to 0.6 and 1.5 to 6, not flagged at 3x, not below 1 while paused). test/e2e/transcode.mjs: 78 s to reach 60 s of film, and the 5 s and 6 s stand-stills.

Each replacement passes on the unchanged application code and fails on a faulty copy of it with that mechanism removed: one faulty copy for each mechanism named below, each failed by the new check alone and not by a clock, none committed.
Each replacement gives the same verdict on a slow runner: it passes with the test, its workers and their ffmpeg held to two CPUs, and no case is dropped or failed for the number of cores.
No test is deleted, and each test that held a bar keeps every assertion it made that reads no clock.

Workers sharing a slow film, checked with two workers and with three: every worker made segments, no segment was made by two jobs, and jobs on different workers were running at the same moment. It fails when no helper starts, and when the workers make their chunks one after another.

The 4K HDR10 copy with TrueHD: the run decoded and encoded no video frame, and ffmpeg was given the arguments that keep the TrueHD's decoding off the video's path. It fails on a copy that decodes or re-encodes the picture, and on one that decodes the audio in the video's path.

A killed worker's job: the replacement was claimed by the other worker before the dead worker's own lease would have run out, and every request of the viewer was answered. It fails on a build that waits the lease out.

A helper that is killed, a helper stopped for another viewer, and a seek into a helper's chunk: the check is which job made each segment of that chunk (a replacement on another worker from the first segment missing; the viewer's own job after a preemption; the helper itself on a seek, with no job started) and that no request of the viewer failed. Each fails on a build where that job does not make them.

A subtitle asked for while chapter pictures fill their slots: it was read while that many chapter jobs were still running and none had finished since it was asked for. It fails on a build where chapter pictures may take every slot.

A shown speed (EncodeSpeed and Framerate in TranscodingInfo on both replicas, jellyscale_transcode_job_speed_ratio) is checked against what the worker recorded for the job, and against itself across a pause at the lead (not lower after than before); IsBelowRealTime is checked against that speed for one job the test keeps below 1 and one it keeps above. No check needs the runner to encode faster than the film.

In test/e2e/transcode.mjs the parallel and failover scenarios judge by what happened: a helper on another worker made segments past the seam that the player then played, the surviving worker took the job over, no request failed or was abandoned, no error dialog showed, and the buffer has no gap at the seam.

Every timing a bar measured is still measured and logged with what it is (the speedup of two and three workers over one, the copy's multiple of real time, kill to first segment, slowest wait, time to reach 60 s, longest stand-still); no test passes, fails or branches on one.

A time bound stays only where it stops a hang: a wait for an event with a timeout (waitFor, a context deadline, a select on time.After), or a measured bound of at least ten times what a right build takes at that step whose wrong build never delivers, or not before a timer or sleep the test set. A bound closer than that is a bar.
The change touches only test files, test scripts and docs: no file the server or a worker is built from.

docs/testing.md says that tests check mechanisms, not speeds, gives the rule for a time bound that may stay, and names where a run's logged timings are kept; what it says holds for a run that passed, locally and in CI.
userStories.notes: Timing bars in the Go tiers, test/e2e and test/roles.sh became checks of what the code did (which worker made each segment, ffmpeg's arguments, job rows); timings are logged and summed by test/report.sh timings. cmd/testreport/timing_test.go fails on any new bar not listed as a hang bound in test/timing-bounds.txt.
